author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Enthusia: making tire grip and vehicle forces visible
summary: The Visual Gravity System in Konami’s 2005 PS2 racing game helps players interpret vehicle behavior. Its indicator adds information that the road view alone cannot provide.
heroAlt: A close-up photograph of a racing tire illustrating the physical subject of grip feedback; not an Enthusia screenshot

sourceLabels.hands-on: Career mode, AI and Driving Revolution hands-on

blocks.text: Show forces the player cannot physically feel

Konami released Enthusia Professional Racing for PS2 in 2005. A television cannot reproduce the bodily sensation of driving a car. The Visual Gravity System, or VGS, supplied a visual aid instead. It represented aspects of vehicle behavior so the player had information beyond the car’s movement across the screen.

The VGS indicator arranged tire information around a central force display. Its changing appearance helped communicate steering and grip behavior. Reading it alongside the road could help a player recognize that the car is beginning to skid. The display represented the game’s vehicle model; it did not measure forces acting on the person holding the controller.
Practice controlling speed at specific points

The Driving Revolution mode required players to pass gates at prescribed speeds. This emphasized preparation, acceleration and braking instead of rewarding only a fast lap. A gate could reveal poor speed control even if the car stayed on the road. The task gave players a repeatable way to practice particular driving actions.

Reports from 2005 also described Enthusia Life and progression through its cars. Together with Driving Revolution, these systems gave the game its own structure in a genre associated with Gran Turismo. Their differences are useful historical context. They do not, by themselves, establish that one game’s physics model was objectively superior to another’s.

During a modern replay, preserve a readable HUD and consistent steering input before changing visual settings. Cropping or obscuring the VGS display removes information that the design intended players to use. This is a practical implication of the interface, rather than a claim about a specific emulator defect or a measured performance result.
